Ma Joye - UmGibe [5281]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Umgibe is a story of Ma’ Joye who was diagnosed with cancer in 2014 as a result she could not work to provide food for her family.
She decided to grow organic vegetables in her backyard.
Just as she was about to harvest her crop, she came out one morning and the chickens had eaten all of the spinach that she had grown.
Overwhelmed by the odds against her she was devastated and went to bed for 3 days.
She had to come up with a solution and thought that she would hang packets in the trees so that the chickens could not reach them.
While she was sitting in her yard she noticed an old ladder and remembered the UmGibe, which was a rack that was used in traditional huts to hang the grass mats off the ground so that the termites would not eat them.
Imbetween the slats of the ladder she suspended plastic bags and raised the ladder off the ground.
So she devised a Frugal Climate Smart system to grow organic vegetables that is raised approximately 80 cm off the ground. Using recycled plastic bags attached to a recycled plastic structure, the system requires less water, expands space, and is portable. Specifically designed for urban farmers, the system is eco-friendly, using organic pesticides and compost for plant nutrients.

Armed with his solution Umgibe provided the much-needed protection from the chickens but it did not end there it saved water and fed the family as well as neighbors who started buying the surplus produce.
Before long Ma Joye was teaching other community members to grow nutritious vegetables.The story that began with pain has now paved the way for the hundreds of families.
A platform was born where poor communities started growing vegetables to feed themselves and collectively sell their surplus produce.
Umgibe is the rope of hope that pulls unemployed and underserved communities up.

Umgibe now works with 497 families and 51 cooperatives and provides training & equipment, as well as market access through restaurant chains and government departments


Nonhlanhla is undoubtedly a role model to South Africans, particularly to women, who can relate to her against-all-odds story. She hopes that her work will serve as an example to women. “I would like teach women that the past has already been written, that they have the power to write the future based on who they are and what they do now,” she says. “There is no better person to rely on than yourself. I learnt that the hard way. Make sure the work that you choose to do is what you feel passionate about; success will follow.”

Awards won
• 2017 SABF Social Innovation Development Award Winner
• 2017 WIA Award (Women In Africa, Morroco
• 2017 SAG –SEED Award Winner (https://www.seed.uno/awards/all/2017/umgibe-frugal-waterwise-growing-system.html)
• 2017 Top Entrepreneur Processing Sector Award -Agriculture & Rural Development (KZN Povince)
• 2017 Marie Claire Future Shaper Awards (SA)
• 2017 Hivos Most Impactful Business Award Winner on Food Security – Harare, Zimbabwe
• 2017 Ecologic-Eco -Community Gold Award Winner – Pretoria, South Africa
• 2017 Ecologic – Eco-Angel Gold Award Winner – Pretoria, South Africa
• 2017 IMPACT2 Global Female Entrepreneur of The Year Award– (Paris, France)
• 2017 ELLE Magazine IMPACT 2 Award Winner (SA winner)
• 2016 Durban Business Fair Rural and Township Based Business Award
• 2016 KZN DARD Female Entrepreneur 1st Runner -Up Provincial Level

Nonhlanhla Joye Script

V/O
Nonhlanhla Joye was born in a rural area of KZN to a family in tune with nature and living off the land.

Ma Joye
“I remember that the most important thing at home was farming and I hated it.”

Mac
“Why did you hate it?”

Ma Joye
“Because it was work, other people were playing and I was working. But what I didn’t know at that time, was that my parents were teaching me to be self sustainable.’

V/O
It worked. Now in her fifties, she’s a crusader. She believes the earth can meet all our needs.

Her efforts to eradicate hunger have been globally acknowledged.

“I know what my purpose now, most people die without ever knowing what their purpose in life is but I feel blessed.”

V/O
Although born into a world that would later bring her accolades, Ma Joye took time to find her path. After school she did domestic work, studied Human Resource Management part time and struggled with the realities of South Africa life.

Ma Joye
“I am a survivor. I have gone through a lot of things in my life. One of them being that I was raped. Not once, not twice but three times and it came a time where I decided I just wanted to leave this country.”

V/O
Leave she did and worked as an au pair in the United States, where she married and had two children.

“That is where I found myself. But I found out that I loved being South African more than I loved anything else.

V/O
On her return she founded an NGO to help heal and empower women. But 4 years ago, disaster struck.

Mac
“At what point did you then know that you had cancer?”

Nonhlanhla
“I developed a lump. At first it was not painful and I would ask the kids to rub it and move on with my life.”

V/O
The cancerous growth was removed, but chemotherapy left her weak. She tapped into her self-preservation skills and returned to Mother Nature.

Ma Joye
“And that’s when I tapped on how I grew up. I never knew you bought vegetables when I grew up.”

Mac
“The same farming that you hated.”

Ma Joye
“The farming that I hated was my saviour at that time and I went and I did the vegetable garden at the back….”

V/O
But bad luck hadn’t finished with Ma Joye. The loss of her entire veggie crop to marauding chickens nearly broke her spirit.


Ma Joye
“And I went on my knees because there was all of my food gone. Chickens, they came and they ate everything. I did not know what to do. I literally cried, because I had no other option.”


V/O
She picked herself up and came up with a plan to elevate her crop to new heights.

Ma Joye
“All I could think was I should use ropes and build a structure and use ropes in order to hang the plastic bags so that I could be able to grow without the chickens touching my vegetables. That’s when I saw that ladder there and I thought about this and that’s how it started.”

V/O
A disused ladder served as a frame to create beds. Then she cast her eyes to the plastic bags littering the countryside.

“So what were people saying when they saw you collecting plastic bags?”

“They thought I was mad. Here is a woman with a shaved head, looking for plastic bags.”

V/O
And so was born Ma Joye’s new farming method - the Umgibe Frugal Vertical System.

“It is frugal but it is climate smart.”

V/O
It’s water-friendly and wheelchair friendly – a necessity at the time for Ma Joye.

“During that time, I was sick, I was a little bit frail and I couldn’t stand for a long time.”

V/O
As time passed, she grew stronger and was able to distribute and even sell surplus stock. She began teaching others to grow food and become independent.

“It means that the food insecurity will be a thing of the past, because everyone could be able to harvest.”


Link
This may look like a simple food garden but it is far more than that. This community garden has restored these ladies pride and dignity.

Zodwa
Before Mama Joye we had nothing. She came and opened our eyes. When we woke up in the morning, we had nothing to do every day but the housework. She asked us to start a business with her.

V/O
Zodwa Mabaso is a member of Ma Joye’s co-operative. Here women work together and share profits, transforming old dumping sites into profitable gardens.

Zodwa
“Life is better because there is money in my bank account every month.”
“I have never farmed before, now I see that there is a future in farming.”

V/O
Their organics vegetables are even sold online. Donna Barnard is one of their buyers.

“So whether you are a city dweller or rural dweller you can actually grown your own organic vegetables. So definitely as far as sustainability is concerned she is onto something here.”

V/O
Ma Joye’s scheme, devised during the depths of despair, has become a platform for the poor, providing income to 600 families across KZN. Richmond resident Busi Sindane markets her produce via Umgibe.

“This helps me to pay my children’s school fees. Before this I could not afford to pay for them. Our life is much better now, before I found Umgibe it was hard. Now I can provide for my children.”

Link
Ma Joye’s passion to stop hunger lead her to start helping schools make their own food gardens as she believes that no child should go hungry.

V/O
Teacher Linda Baqwa has seen the benefits for hungry learners.

Linda
“And even when you pass as a teacher going to the kitchen to warm up your food. You will see that their eyes give you the language that “Miss I am hungry”, but you cannot feed the school with one lunch box.”

V/O
With Ma Joye’s guidance, learners are growing their own food to fill their lunch-boxes and tummies.

Mac
“What changes have you seen in the students?”

Linda
“Some of the stuff that we have already got from the garden we gave to children that are affected. They went home and cooked the stuff, we are happy because on their grades they have improved.”

V/O
To celebrate women’s month, 100 girls from 10 schools spent time at the Umgibe farm, enjoying a lunch from the soil.

“Let’s become that village, that raises these children and to say we acknowledge you, we love you , we want to take care of you, we want to support you, but more than anything we want to teach you to be self sustainable.”

Link
All that Mama Joye wanted to do was to feed her family, but little did she know that her Umgibe garden would bring her fame and international awards.

V/O
Her methods have been recognized from Morocco to Paris and back and she has won 12 awards for her work in eradicating hunger.

Ma Joye
“And to be among the women that are doing that in a global space, that also said “Go ahead do this.” You are on the right path. It talks to my purpose to stop hunger.”

Mac
“Was your cancer eventually cured?”

Nonhlanhla
“I am healthier than you are today, yes, thank God for that.”

“This didn’t start as a business, it started as something to survive and I know it restored my dignity.


Promo 1 – 15 secs
How did Nonhlanhla Joye rise from cancer sufferer to global award winner? Meet an inspirational woman who has created gold in her fields of green.

Promo 2 - 15

“It started as something to survive.”
Ma Joye was diagnosed with cancer 4 years ago, so turned to the soil. Now she’s a major supplier of organic vegetables and her Umgibe farming system has empowered hundreds of families in KZN.

Promo 3 - 10 secs
As a child, Nonhlanhla Joye hated farming. But it was a skill that in later years would save her life and that of hundreds of families across KZN.
